column11: Regarding which it is said (Proverbs 17:16): "Wherefore is there a price in the hand of a fool to get wisdom, seeing he has no heart?", which the Sages expounded in Yoma (72b) concerning one who possesses Torah but lacks fear of Heaven, that is, the heartfelt recognition that "I have set Hashem always before me" [Psalms 16:8], through which awe is generated, as written in the gloss of Rema (Orach Chayim 1:1), and this is "they have forsaken Me," having abandoned Him from his memory, whereupon the Blessed Name likewise abandons him from His remembrance.

column9: Shabbat 88b: ‘And that is what Rava said: To those who are right-handed in their approach to Torah, and engage in its study with strength, good will, and sanctity, Torah is a drug of life, and to those who are left-handed in their approach to Torah, it is a drug of death. column11: And nonetheless, after death it is scoured completely by the power of teshuvah — even the sin of chillul Hashem, the gravest of all; for all that teshuvah does not avail to scour completely is only from the side of this world, [whereas] teshuvah is from the power of binah — “his heart understands and returns” — which is the secret of the World to Come.
column13: And poured forth supernal lovingkindness beyond mortal capacity, necessarily dissolving them. As occurred in the Flood, pouring water in overwhelming torrents until they could not contain such great kindness and were wiped out; for the root of water is Chesed (Zohar Terumah 159b), yet descending without measure it becomes destructive to the recipient.

column9: Zohar, Miketz 12:194-206: ‘Alas for that day, a day of wrath and indignation! Hence it behoves man to contend daily with his evil prompter and to picture to himself the day when he will stand before the King to be judged, when they will lower him into the ground to rot there, whilst the soul will become separated from him. We have been taught that it behoves man always to rouse the good prompter against the evil prompter; if the latter departs, well and good, but if not, the man should study the Torah, as there is nothing so well calculated to crush the evil prompter as the Torah; if he departs, well and good, but if not, let the man remind him of the day of death so as thereby to subdue him.’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 8 — Increasing or Decreasing: Beit Hillel and Beit Shammai, Rav Tzadok cites this kabbalistic teaching (Zohar, Miketz 12:194-206) to illuminate his statement here (“as written in the Holy Zohar (Part I, 202a): "For you have no instrument to shatter the Evil Inclination except Torah"; and so they stated (ibid. 190a): "When a man sees unholy thoughts approaching him, let him...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, divine service, and the rectification of the heart developed in this discourse of Pri Tzaddik.
column11: Yet all of it derived from cynicism toward the truth, forging a falsehood that mimics the truth. And this is likewise the nature of the idolatry of Ba'al Pe'or (Bamidbar 25:3); directly opposite which Moshe Rabbeinu was buried, he being the root of the Torah called by his name (Malachi 3:22), which is the exact antithesis of mockery, as written: "when a word of Torah enters, a word of scoffing departs" (Shir HaShirim Rabbah 1:2); and automatically the power of Pe'or is nullified, which represents the extreme nadir of cynicism.
column13: In truth, goodness existed in this tree as well, but while in other trees good was clearly distinguishable from evil, in this tree good appeared as evil, defying easy discernment. For the early generations lacked moral discernment, and good often appeared as evil; as we see with King David, whose entire seventy years were gifted by Adam (Zohar Vayishlach 168b); and yet, as the Zohar states (Shemini 40b), David loved judgment, which is why even Samuel, the greatest of prophets, initially misjudged him.

column11: And in the first chapter of Yoma [9b]: "They were wicked, yet they placed their trust in the Holy One, blessed be He", for such an attitude is not true trust—to assume that despite sinning, the Holy One is with him, since this only breeds flippancy toward committing sin; and even if he observes fortune favoring him at the moment, did they not rule in Bava Kamma [50a]: "Whoever says the Holy One, blessed be He, is forgiving [of sin without consequence], his life shall be relinquished" etc.
column13: “And call the Sabbath a delight (oneg)”—delight means that man yearns exclusively for the illumination of the Countenance of the Blessed Name; and the exact reverse of oneg is nega , as stated in Sefer Yetzirah (2:4): “There is nothing in goodness higher than oneg, and nothing in evil lower than nega,” and nega signifies that a person fled from before his Master, as stated in the Holy Zohar (Tazria 49b): “the shutting off of supernal light.”

column9: Arakhin 10b: ‘The Gemara objects: On the New Moon, which is called an appointed day, let us say hallel. The Gemara explains: The New Moon is not sanctified with regard to the prohibition against the performance of labor, and hallel is recited only on a day that is sanctified, as it is written: “You shall have a song as in the night when a festival is sanctified” (Isaiah 30:29), which indicates that a night that is sanctified as a Festival, which includes a prohibition of labor, requires song, but one that is not sanctified as a Festival does not require song.’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 9 — The Chanukah Celebration and the Meaning of Dedication, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Arakhin 10b) to illuminate his statement here (“for it states (Arachin 10b): "Shabbat, etc., is not called an appointed festival (mo'ed); Rosh Chodesh, etc., is not sanctified with the prohibition of labor, etc.; a night sanctified for the festival requires song,...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, divine service, and the rectification of the heart developed in this discourse of Pri Tzaddik.
column11: And Saul, who likewise attained this "glory of kings," ascended beyond his appropriate spiritual level, presuming to delve into the hidden counsel of Hashem, which was never granted to human intellect to fathom; assuming that unto kings permission was granted to investigate even this deepest mystery; and that Shmuel, whose perception was prophetic vision, did not perceive the path of extracting the holy spark from Amalek because he did not know of any earthly revelation for it.
column13: And this enduring distinction is termed “a song for the Sabbath day.” For behold, the Blessed Name created the cosmos out of the abundance of His lovingkindness without any awakening or initiative from man below. And likewise Hashem appointed a boundary and culmination for all creation, that all things will return and be reabsorbed into their Source without human knowledge or initiative, as it is said (Isaiah 2:11): “And the Lord alone shall be exalted on that day,” leaving no separate, independent existence for any creature.

column9: Shabbat 119a: ‘The Exilarch said to Rav Hamnuna: What is the meaning of that which is written, “The holy one of God is honored” (Isaiah 58:13)? Rav Hamnuna said to him: That is Yom Kippur, when there is no eating or drinking, and so the Torah said: Honor it with a clean garment. And with regard to that which is stated about Shabbat, “And you shall honor it,” Rav said: To honor Shabbat, make the Shabbat feast earlier than on other days, in order to show that one delights in eating it. And Shmuel said: To honor Shabbat, make the Shabbat feast later, so that one’s appetite will be greater. The sons of Rav Pappa bar Abba said to Rav Pappa: People like us, for whom meat and wine is found on our table every…’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 9 — The Chanukah Celebration and the Meaning of Dedication, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 119a) to illuminate his statement here (“However, the expression "made them" is patterned after what we find (Shabbat 119a, Kiddushin 31a): "I will make a festive day for the Rabbis", and Rashi explained: "a feast"; and we explained that the intention in...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, divine service, and the rectification of the heart developed in this discourse of Pri Tzaddik.
column11: However, 'rivo' myriad/ten thousand is not merely a number, rather an expression of boundless multitude; for ten everywhere is a complete and filled number, filling and encompassing everything from beginning to end as noted in section 55; therefore the completion of multitude is ten thousand; and a thousand is the culmination of standard counting, while a myriad revavah is its boundless perfection.

column13: And akin to what we find in Hashem's promise to Israel: that through observing His commandments they will prolong days, which indicates that man holds an integrated grasp in Hashem's blessing. And the parable for this is: if an overwhelming fortune is given to a person all at once, his former equilibrium is shattered, and this is not a whole goodness; however if it is given gradually, stage after stage, then even when he stands at the highest pinnacle he remembers his youth and the smaller steps preceding that hour.

column9: Kiddushin 31a: ‘Rav Yosef, who was blind, said: At first I would say: If someone would tell me that the halakha is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda, who says: A blind person is exempt from fulfilling the mitzvot, I would make a festive day for the rabbis, as I am not commanded and yet I perform the mitzvot. And through the practical performance of the mitzvot, wherein one serves with the vitality and intellectual grasp available to one's delimited heart and contracted mind, serving the Life of all worlds, the Living God and Sovereign of Eternity, the inner spark of life dwelling within him unites and binds directly with the Primal Source of Life.
column13: Yet while Adam, the direct handiwork of God, has no explicit teshuvah recorded in Torah, Cain who was the second generation was required to repent, as recorded: “My punishment is greater than I can bear.” In the generation of Enosh, however, the Blessed Name instituted active concealment so that creation might be fortified; for the enduring existence of creation depends upon concealment, through which moral service and exaltation arise when fulfilling mitzvot, alongside shame and retribution when violating them.

column9: Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 670:2: “Taz (Orach Chayim 670:3, citing the Levush) explains why Purim has an obligation of festive meals (mishteh ve-simchah) whereas Chanukah’s primary obligation is Hallel and praise rather than feasting: on Purim Haman decreed to annihilate the physical bodies of Israel, so the salvation is celebrated with bodily feasting; on Chanukah the Greeks sought to uproot the soul and the Torah while leaving the body intact if Israel assimilated, so the salvation is celebrated through spiritual praise and the light of Torah.” Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 9 — The Chanukah Celebration and the Meaning of Dedication, Rav Tzadok cites this commentary and halakhic exposition (Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 670:2) to illuminate his statement here (“And the Taz (Section 670, subsection 3) cited from the Levush that on Purim physical salvation occurred, and therefore it contains a mitzvah of feasting, unlike Chanukah where the Greeks decreed only spiritual...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, divine service, and the rectification of the heart developed in this discourse of Pri Tzaddik.
column11: And this current exile preparing for the World to Come is the drawing of blood and the beginning of healing, and when the healing of the world's mortal stroke is completed, we will merit the World to Come—the mystery of the eighth day— which is the perfection of the covenant in the flesh, the body being consecrated to enter the Supernal Land and merit eternal life.
column13: Yet the raw physical frame in itself holds no natural affinity to the soul; thus the body can dissolve while the soul endures; whereas had the Blessed Name dwelt directly within the body without an intermediary, the body could never disintegrate. So too exists an intermediary between the Blessed Name and heaven and earth: this intermediary is the word “et” written between “Elohim” and “the heavens,” for “et” (from Aleph to Tav) alludes to the Sovereignty of Heaven (Malchut), embodying His underlying Will in creation.

column11: He being the father who bestows, and they the recipients of life from him, which is the meaning of "eating bread." column13: “His favor that He reveals unto him”— meaning when Hashem reveals before man's eyes whom He chooses and favors at present, then: “to nullify all shells,” so that all are dissolved. And so Scripture states (Psalms 30:11): “Hear, Hashem, and be gracious unto me; Hashem, be my helper”: “Hear, Hashem, and be gracious unto me” is in the aspect of bread, the sustenance of the heart, for even this is Hashem's salvation that man perceive this; “Hashem, be my helper” is in the aspect of gladdening wine.

column9: Midrash Tanchuma, Noach 3: ‘The Israelites did not accept the Torah until the Holy One, blessed be He, arched the mountain over them like a vessel, as it is said: And they stood beneath the mountain (Exod. 19:17). R. Dimi the son of Hama stated that the Holy One, blessed be He, told Israel: If you accept the Torah, well and good; but if not, your grave will be there. If you should say that He arched the mountain over them because of the Written Law, isn’t it true that as soon as He said to them, “Will you accept the Torah?” they all responded, “We will do and hear,” because the Written Law was brief and required no striving and suffering, but rather He threatened them because of the Oral Law. After all, it contains…’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 9 — The Chanukah Celebration and the Meaning of Dedication, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Midrash Tanchuma, Noach 3) to illuminate his statement here (“as stated (Midrash Tanchuma Noach 3) that anyone who loves physical luxury cannot master the Oral Torah, because it entails great exertion, wandering of sleep, etc. And likewise Yom Kippur, as stated in Chapter 4 of...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, divine service, and the rectification of the heart developed in this discourse of Pri Tzaddik.
column11: Alongside the fact that the initial acceptance of the Torah at Sinai was under duress ("He suspended the mountain over them"). Not so regarding the second entry during the Second Temple, when they reaccepted the Torah willingly in the days of Ahasuerus (Shabbat 88a), and were righteous to the degree that they were worthy of open miracles: this corresponds to "this people whom You have acquired," through a binding transaction (kinyan) which is an exchange of value for value through their own merit, rather than an unearned gift.
column13: Therefore prior to this Adam was not commanded regarding the Tree of Knowledge, for he was like an unborn child that produces no waste and cannot sin. Only after Adam prayed for rain on behalf of all creations, bringing creation from potential into actualized deed, as in Chullin (60b): “This teaches that the vegetation stood at the threshold of the soil” — did the true birth of Adam in this world take place, attaining maturity as an agent of free choice, capable of acting contrary to the divine Will.
